after: ## Step 0: is this a consumer contract?
alt: A trader (section 2(2)) acts for trade, business, craft or professional purposes; a consumer (section 2(3)) is an individual acting wholly or mainly outside them, so a company is never a consumer. A plumber buying a kettle for home use is covered; the same plumber buying a pipe cutter for work, a business-to-business contract, and a private sale between individuals are not.
caption: Check trader and consumer first: otherwise these sections do not apply.

after: ## Terms implied into contracts to supply goods
alt: Three implied terms. Section 9, satisfactory quality, judged by a reasonable person (Rogers v Parish). Section 10, fitness for a particular purpose made known to the trader (Priest v Last; Griffiths v Peter Conway, where the purpose was not made known). Section 11, goods must match their description (Beale v Taylor). Grant v Australian Knitting Mills breached both sections 9 and 10.
caption: Quality, fitness for purpose and description: automatic terms in every goods contract.

after: ## Terms implied into contracts to supply goods
alt: The aspects of quality in section 9(3): fitness for usual purposes, appearance and finish, freedom from minor defects, safety and durability. The test is objective and flexible, and public statements can be relevant. Section 9(4) excludes defects drawn to the consumer’s attention, defects an examination ought to have revealed, and in a sale by sample defects a reasonable examination of the sample would have revealed.
caption: Quality is judged objectively; defects the consumer was told of or should have spotted are excluded.

alt: Three tiers of goods remedies. Tier 1, section 20 with 22: short-term right to reject, normally within 30 days, full refund. Tier 2, section 23: repair or replacement chosen by the consumer, at the trader’s cost. Tier 3, section 24: price reduction or final right to reject, only after one failed repair or replacement or if repair and replacement are impossible, disproportionate or not done properly.
caption: Reject within 30 days; after that, repair or replace first, then price reduction or final rejection.

alt: A timeline from delivery: the short-term right to reject runs for 30 days, and a fault appearing within six months is presumed to have existed on delivery. Three rules: the 30-day clock stops while a repair or replacement is awaited, with at least seven days left afterwards; the six-month presumption; and no deduction for use under the final right to reject within six months, except for motor vehicles.
caption: Thirty days to reject; six months in which faults are presumed present from delivery.

alt: Two services terms: section 49, reasonable care and skill, about how the work is done; section 52, performance within a reasonable time where none is fixed (Charnock v Liverpool Corporation). Remedies: section 55 repeat performance at the trader’s cost, then section 56 price reduction up to the full price. Lateness under section 52 goes straight to a price reduction.
caption: Poor work: repeat performance, then a price reduction. Lateness: a price reduction.

alt: Rhian’s laptop: a consumer contract; arguably breaches sections 9 and 10; at 40 days the short-term right has gone but the six-month presumption applies; after one failed repair she can use section 24. Her bathroom: uneven tiling breaches section 49 and four months may breach section 52; she can require repeat performance under section 55, then a price reduction under section 56, which is also the remedy for delay.
caption: Goods and services follow separate terms and separate remedy ladders.
